about: Fluid Mechanics 1 (CIVE40008) is a 5-ECTS core module in Part I (Year 1) of Imperial's Civil Engineering MEng, running across the Autumn and Spring terms (2026–27 programme specification). Imperial does not publish a topic list for it. A third-party copy of the module description (UC Education Abroad, last reviewed 2025–26) says it teaches fluid mechanics for civil engineers, with students producing simplified outline designs of hydraulic structures and estimating wave loads on offshore platforms. The nine topics here are a standard first-year civil engineering fluid mechanics course built from that description, so check them against your own module materials. The programme specification gives only an indicative Year 1 split of 32% coursework and 68% examination across all modules, not this module's own assessment.
topics: Hydrostatic forces on dams, gates and walls
Conservation of mass and energy: Bernoulli, orifices and flow measurement
The momentum principle: forces on gates, nozzles and bends
Pipe flow: Reynolds number and head losses
Open-channel flow: uniform flow, specific energy and critical depth
Wave loads on offshore structures: the Morison equation

notes.h: Fluid properties and pressure in still water
notes.body:
Civil engineers deal mostly with water: in rivers, reservoirs, pipes, sewers and the sea. This topic sets out the properties used throughout the module and how pressure varies in water at rest.

What makes a fluid
- A fluid deforms continuously under any shear stress. At rest it carries no shear, only pressure, which acts normal to every surface.
- We treat water as a continuum and, for almost all civil engineering problems, as incompressible (bulk modulus about 2.2 GPa).

Properties you will use (typical values)
- Density ρ: fresh water ≈ 1000 kg/m³; sea water ≈ 1025 kg/m³; mercury ≈ 13 600 kg/m³.
- Specific weight γ = ρg: about 9.81 kN/m³ for fresh water.
- Dynamic viscosity μ (water ≈ 1.0 × 10⁻³ Pa s at 20 °C) and kinematic viscosity ν = μ/ρ (≈ 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m²/s). Viscosity of water falls noticeably as temperature rises.
- Newton's law of viscosity: τ = μ du/dy. Water and air are Newtonian; many muds, slurries and fresh concrete are not.
- Surface tension (≈ 0.073 N/m for water): important for small-scale models and capillary rise in soils, usually negligible at full scale.
- Vapour pressure: if pressure falls below it, cavitation occurs (a concern on spillways, in pumps and at siphon crests).

The hydrostatic law
Vertical equilibrium of a small column of fluid gives dp/dz = −ρg (z upwards). For water of constant density:
p = p_atm + ρgh, where h is depth below the free surface.
- Pressure depends only on depth, not on the shape of the container.
- At the same level in a continuous body of still water, the pressure is the same.
- Gauge pressure (relative to atmosphere) is ρgh; absolute pressure adds about 101 kPa.

Pressure head
Engineers often express pressure as an equivalent height of water: h = p/(ρg). For example, 50 kPa corresponds to 50 000/(1000 × 9.81) ≈ 5.10 m of water. Water-supply pressures, pump heads and reservoir levels are all quoted in metres.

Worked example: deep water
Gauge pressure 30 m below the sea surface:
- p = 1025 × 9.81 × 30 ≈ 302 kPa (about 3 atmospheres above atmospheric).
- In fresh water at the same depth it would be 294 kPa.
- The absolute pressure in sea water is about 302 + 101 = 403 kPa.

Measuring pressure
- Piezometer: an open tube; the water rises to the pressure head.
- U-tube manometer: uses a denser fluid for larger pressures. Work through the fluids from one end to the other, adding ρgh going down and subtracting ρgh going up.
- Bourdon gauges and electronic transducers are used in the field; they read gauge pressure.

Why it matters in civil engineering
Hydrostatic pressure governs loads on dams, retaining walls, lock gates, basement walls and tanks, the uplift under foundations and dams, and the pressure available in water distribution networks.

Exam tips: state whether pressures are gauge or absolute; use the right density (sea water in coastal and offshore problems); convert kPa to Pa before dividing by ρg.

Outline design of dams, sluice and lock gates, weirs and retaining walls starts with the hydrostatic force and where it acts.

Plane surfaces
- For any plane surface, the resultant force is F = ρ g h_c A, where h_c is the depth of the centroid of the wetted area.
- It acts normal to the surface at the centre of pressure, which lies below the centroid for any non-horizontal surface (on a horizontal surface the pressure is uniform and the two coincide): y_cp = y_c + I_c/(y_c A), measured along the plane from the free-surface line.
- For a vertical wall retaining water of depth h (per metre run): the pressure diagram is a triangle, F = ρgh²/2, acting at h/3 above the base.

Worked example: dam face
Water 10 m deep against a vertical dam face, per metre length:
- F = 1000 × 9.81 × 10²/2 = 490.5 kN/m.
- It acts 10/3 = 3.33 m above the base, so the overturning moment about the toe is 490.5 × 3.33 ≈ 1635 kN m/m.

Curved surfaces (radial or Tainter gates, spillway crests)
- Horizontal component = the force on the vertical projection of the surface, with the same line of action.
- Vertical component = the weight of water (real or imaginary) vertically above the curved surface up to the free-surface level.
- For a circular arc, every pressure force is normal to the surface and so passes through the centre of curvature; the resultant does too. This is why radial gates are hinged at the centre of curvature: the water force has no moment about the hinge, so the gate is easy to lift.
- Example: a quarter-circle gate of radius 3 m with the water surface level with its top and the quarter-circle of water lying directly above the curved surface, per metre width: F_H = ρgR²/2 = 44.1 kN/m and F_V = ρgπR²/4 = 69.3 kN/m (the weight of that quarter-circle of water). If the water were instead on the other side of the gate, F_V would be the weight of the imaginary water between the gate and the free-surface level, so check the geometry before using πR²/4, so the resultant is 82.2 kN/m at about 57.5° to the horizontal.

Gravity dam stability (outline design)
A gravity dam resists water thrust by its own weight. Per metre length check:
- Overturning about the toe: factor of safety = restoring moment (weight) / overturning moment (water thrust and uplift). Often at least 1.5 is sought.
- Sliding: factor = μ(W − U)/F, where μ is the base friction coefficient and U the uplift.
- Uplift: water seeping under the dam pushes up on the base. A simple assumption is a triangular distribution from full reservoir head at the heel to zero (or the tailwater head) at the toe. Drains and grout curtains reduce it.
- Middle-third rule: if the resultant force on the base passes within the middle third, the base is in compression everywhere (no tension at the heel). Base pressures are σ = (V/B)(1 ± 6e/B), with e the eccentricity of the resultant from the base centre.

Buoyancy
Archimedes: the upward force on an immersed body equals the weight of fluid displaced. This matters for caissons, pontoons, pipelines laid on the sea bed and basements in high groundwater (flotation or uplift checks).

Exam tips: work per metre length; draw the pressure diagram and use its area and centroid; always include uplift when asked about dam stability; show moments about the toe with clear signs.

notes.h: Continuity, Bernoulli and the energy equation
notes.body:
Moving water is analysed with three conservation laws: mass, energy and momentum. This topic covers the first two.

Continuity
For steady flow of an incompressible fluid, the volume flow rate Q is the same at every section: Q = A₁V₁ = A₂V₂, using mean velocities. In open channels, per metre width, q = Vy is constant (q in m²/s).

Bernoulli's equation
For steady, inviscid, incompressible flow along a streamline:
p/(ρg) + V²/(2g) + z = H (constant)
- p/(ρg) is the pressure head, V²/(2g) the velocity head and z the elevation head; H is the total head.
- Engineers often plot the energy grade line (EGL, height H) and the hydraulic grade line (HGL, height p/(ρg) + z) along a pipeline.

The engineering energy equation
Real flows lose energy to friction and turbulence, and pumps and turbines add or remove it:
H₁ + h_pump = H₂ + h_turbine + h_L
This is the basis of every pipeline, pumping and hydropower calculation.

Flow from tanks: orifices
- Ideal jet speed from a small opening at depth H below the free surface (Torricelli): V = √(2gH).
- Real flow: Q = C_d a √(2gH), where a is the orifice area and C_d the discharge coefficient (about 0.6 for a sharp-edged orifice, because the jet contracts to a vena contracta and loses a little energy).
- Example: a 50 mm sharp-edged orifice under 2 m head with C_d = 0.62: a = 1.96 × 10⁻³ m², √(2gH) = 6.26 m/s, Q ≈ 7.6 L/s (ideal 12.3 L/s).
- Tank draining: as the level falls the flow drops. For a tank of plan area A_t draining through an orifice, the time to fall from H₁ to H₂ is t = 2A_t(√H₁ − √H₂)/(C_d a √(2g)). For a 2 m² tank draining from 2 m to empty through the orifice above, t ≈ 1050 s (about 17.5 minutes).

Flow measurement in pipes
- Venturi meter: a smooth contraction; the pressure drop to the throat gives Q = C_d A₂√{2Δp/[ρ(1 − (A₂/A₁)²)]}, with C_d around 0.95–0.99.
- Orifice plate: simpler but loses much more head.
- Pitot tube: measures stagnation pressure to give local velocity, V = √(2Δp/ρ), used to traverse rivers and pipes.

Flow measurement in channels
Weirs and flumes are introduced in the open-channel topic; they also rely on Bernoulli plus a critical-flow condition.

Assumptions to state
Steady flow, incompressible, negligible losses between the two points (or losses included explicitly), points on the same streamline (or irrotational flow), and hydrostatic pressure across straight, parallel streamlines.

Exam tips: pick points where many terms are known (free surfaces: p = 0 gauge and V ≈ 0 for large reservoirs); use continuity to link velocities; for siphons and pipes over high ground, check that the HGL does not fall more than about 7–8 m below the pipe, or the water may cavitate or release dissolved air.

notes.h: The momentum principle and forces on structures
notes.body:
Bernoulli gives velocities and pressures, but forces on gates, bends, nozzles and piers need the momentum principle: Newton's second law applied to a control volume.

The steady-flow momentum equation
ΣF = ρQ(V_out − V_in)
- ΣF is the sum of all external forces on the fluid inside the control volume: pressure forces at the inflow and outflow sections, the force from any solid boundary, and weight if there is a vertical component.
- It is a vector equation: apply it separately in each direction.
- The force of the water on the structure is equal and opposite to the force of the structure on the water.

Hydrostatic pressure forces in channels
In an open channel with straight, parallel streamlines, the pressure is hydrostatic, so the pressure force on a section of depth y (per metre width) is ρgy²/2.

Sluice gate
Water flows under a vertical sluice gate from a deep, slow upstream section (depth y₁) to a shallow, fast section just downstream (depth y₂, at the vena contracta).
1. Bernoulli (small losses) plus continuity gives q = y₁y₂√[2g/(y₁ + y₂)].
2. Momentum on a control volume between the two sections, with F_g the force from the gate on the water (acting upstream):
   ½ρgy₁² − ½ρgy₂² − F_g = ρq(V₂ − V₁)
   so F_g = ½ρg(y₁² − y₂²) − ρq(V₂ − V₁).
Worked example: y₁ = 2.0 m, y₂ = 0.4 m.
- q = 2.0 × 0.4 × √(19.62/2.4) ≈ 2.29 m²/s; V₁ = 1.14 m/s; V₂ = 5.72 m/s.
- Hydrostatic difference: ½ × 9810 × (4 − 0.16) ≈ 18.8 kN/m.
- Momentum change: 1000 × 2.29 × (5.72 − 1.14) ≈ 10.5 kN/m.
- Force on the gate ≈ 18.8 − 10.5 ≈ 8.4 kN/m (downstream).
The force is much less than the hydrostatic thrust of a still pool of depth 2 m (19.6 kN/m) because the water accelerates under the gate and the pressure on the gate's lower part drops.

Nozzles and bends in pipes
- A nozzle on a fire hose or a jetting pipe experiences a force that tends to pull it off the hose, found from the momentum equation with the inlet pressure force.
- Pipe bends on water mains need thrust blocks or restrained joints to resist the resultant of pressure forces and momentum change; in large mains the pressure terms dominate.

Jets on surfaces
- A jet of area A and speed V striking a fixed flat plate normally exerts F = ρAV².
- Turning a jet through an angle changes its momentum and produces a force on the vane, which is the principle of impulse turbines.

Exam tips: draw the control volume and every force on the water, including the hydrostatic forces at each section; use the momentum equation where energy losses are unknown (as in a hydraulic jump) and Bernoulli where losses are negligible (as under a sluice gate).

notes.h: Flow in pipes: Reynolds number and head losses
notes.body:
Water supply, sewer rising mains, pumped drainage and hydropower penstocks all need head losses in pipes to be predicted.

Laminar or turbulent?
The Reynolds number Re = VD/ν compares inertial to viscous effects.
- Re below about 2000: laminar (smooth layers).
- Re above about 4000: turbulent (strong mixing).
- Water mains are almost always turbulent: water at 1.4 m/s in a 300 mm pipe has Re ≈ 1.4 × 0.3/10⁻⁶ ≈ 4 × 10⁵.

Friction losses: Darcy–Weisbach
h_f = f (L/D) V²/(2g)
- f is the (Darcy) friction factor. For laminar flow f = 64/Re.
- For turbulent flow f depends on Re and relative roughness k_s/D (k_s is the equivalent sand roughness of the pipe wall). The Colebrook–White equation, 1/√f = −2 log₁₀[k_s/(3.7D) + 2.51/(Re√f)], describes commercial pipes and is plotted in the Moody diagram. UK practice also uses design charts and tables based on Colebrook–White.
- At high Re in rough pipes f becomes independent of Re (rough turbulent flow).
- Because V = 4Q/(πD²), at a fixed flow and friction factor h_f is proportional to 1/D⁵: halving the diameter multiplies the friction loss by 32. This makes pipe diameter the key design decision.

Local (minor) losses
h_m = K V²/(2g) at entrances (K ≈ 0.5 for a sharp entrance), exits into reservoirs (K = 1), bends, valves and junctions. In long mains these are small compared with friction; in short pipe runs, pumping stations and treatment works they can dominate.

Worked example: a trunk main
Q = 0.1 m³/s through a 300 mm main, 1000 m long, f = 0.018.
- A = 0.0707 m², V = 1.41 m/s, V²/(2g) = 0.102 m.
- h_f = 0.018 × (1000/0.3) × 0.102 ≈ 6.1 m (a pressure drop of about 60 kPa).

Pipe networks and systems
- Series: same Q; head losses add.
- Parallel: same head loss across each branch; flows add. A second (parallel) main is a common way to reinforce capacity.
- Networks: at each junction flows balance; around each loop head losses sum to zero (the basis of the Hardy Cross method and of modern network software).

Pumps and system curves
- The system curve gives the head needed for each flow: static lift plus losses, which rise roughly with Q².
- The pump operates where its head–flow curve crosses the system curve.
- Power to the water = ρgQH; shaft power = ρgQH/η.

Exam tips: compute Re to confirm the regime; keep D in metres; when f must be found from Re and roughness, start with a guess (0.02) and iterate; include exit losses when a pipe discharges into a reservoir.

notes.h: Open-channel flow: uniform flow, specific energy and critical depth
notes.body:
Rivers, canals, culverts, sewers flowing part-full and spillways all have a free surface at atmospheric pressure. Gravity drives the flow, and the depth is free to change.

Key terms
- Hydraulic radius R = A/P, where A is the flow area and P the wetted perimeter (the length of wetted boundary, not including the free surface). For a rectangular channel of width b and depth y: R = by/(b + 2y).
- Uniform flow: depth and velocity do not change along the channel; gravity is balanced by bed friction, and the water surface is parallel to the bed.
- The Froude number Fr = V/√(gy) (for a rectangular channel) compares flow speed with the speed of small surface waves. Fr < 1: subcritical (deep, slow, tranquil); Fr > 1: supercritical (shallow, fast, rapid); Fr = 1: critical.

Manning's equation (uniform flow, SI units)
V = (1/n) R^(2/3) S^(1/2), Q = AV
- n is Manning's roughness coefficient (around 0.012–0.015 for concrete, higher for natural channels with vegetation).
- S is the bed slope.
- Example: rectangular concrete channel b = 4 m, y = 1.5 m, n = 0.015, S = 0.001. A = 6 m², P = 7 m, R = 0.857 m, V = 1.90 m/s, Q ≈ 11.4 m³/s, Fr ≈ 0.50 (subcritical). The depth for a given Q is the normal depth.

Specific energy
Energy measured above the channel bed: E = y + V²/(2g) = y + q²/(2gy²) for a rectangular channel (q = Q/b).
- For a given q, the E–y curve has a minimum. Each E above the minimum can occur at two depths (alternate depths): one subcritical and one supercritical.
- At the minimum the flow is critical: y_c = (q²/g)^(1/3), V_c = √(gy_c), and E_min = 1.5y_c.
- Example: q = 2 m²/s gives y_c = (4/9.81)^(1/3) ≈ 0.742 m and E_min ≈ 1.11 m.

Using critical flow: weirs, flumes and transitions
- A raised bed (a hump) reduces the specific energy available. In subcritical flow the water surface drops over the hump; if the hump is high enough the flow becomes critical over it ("choked").
- Critical depth gives a unique depth–discharge relation, so it is used for measurement. For an ideal broad-crested weir with upstream energy head H above the crest: Q = b √g (2H/3)^(3/2) ≈ 1.705 b H^(3/2) (SI units), reduced in practice by a discharge coefficient.
- Venturi flumes (contractions in width) work the same way.

Control and flow profiles
Subcritical flow is controlled from downstream (e.g. by a weir or reservoir), supercritical flow from upstream (e.g. by a sluice gate). Gradually varied flow profiles connect these controls; when supercritical flow must return to subcritical, a hydraulic jump forms.

Exam tips: always work out Fr to classify the flow; for rectangular channels use q per unit width; remember that in Manning's equation R is a length in metres and the units are SI-specific.

A hydraulic jump is an abrupt rise in water level where fast, shallow supercritical flow changes to slow, deep subcritical flow. It is turbulent and dissipates a lot of energy, which is exactly why engineers create jumps on purpose below spillways and sluice gates.

Why momentum, not energy
Inside the jump there is intense turbulence and an unknown energy loss, so Bernoulli cannot be used across it. Momentum still applies: over a short length of horizontal channel, bed friction is negligible and the only forces are the hydrostatic forces at each end.

The conjugate (sequent) depth equation
For a rectangular channel, per metre width, momentum between section 1 (before) and 2 (after):
½ρgy₁² − ½ρgy₂² = ρq(V₂ − V₁)
Using q = V₁y₁ = V₂y₂ and simplifying:
y₂/y₁ = ½[√(1 + 8Fr₁²) − 1], where Fr₁ = V₁/√(gy₁).
The same equation works backwards (swap 1 and 2) to find the upstream depth from a known downstream depth.

Energy loss in the jump
ΔE = E₁ − E₂ = (y₂ − y₁)³/(4y₁y₂)
This is always positive when y₂ > y₁, confirming that a jump can only go from supercritical to subcritical.

Worked example (following the sluice gate in the momentum topic)
Flow leaves a sluice gate at y₁ = 0.4 m with q = 2.29 m²/s, so V₁ = 5.72 m/s.
- Fr₁ = 5.72/√(9.81 × 0.4) ≈ 2.89 (supercritical).
- y₂ = 0.2 × [√(1 + 8 × 2.89²) − 1] ≈ 1.45 m.
- V₂ = 2.29/1.45 ≈ 1.58 m/s, Fr₂ ≈ 0.42 (subcritical).
- ΔE = (1.45 − 0.4)³/(4 × 0.4 × 1.45) ≈ 0.49 m: about a quarter of the incoming specific energy of 2.07 m is dissipated.
Note that energy conservation would wrongly predict a downstream depth of 2.0 m (the alternate depth), not the conjugate depth.

Types of jump (by upstream Froude number, approximately)
- Fr₁ 1–1.7: undular jump (surface ripples, little loss).
- Fr₁ 1.7–2.5: weak jump.
- Fr₁ 2.5–4.5: oscillating jump (unstable; can create waves that damage banks).
- Fr₁ 4.5–9: steady jump (well formed, preferred for stilling basins).
- Fr₁ above 9: strong jump (very high losses, rough surface).

Engineering uses
- Stilling basins at the foot of spillways and below sluice gates dissipate energy so the river bed downstream is not scoured. Baffle blocks and end sills help hold the jump in place.
- The jump's position depends on the tailwater depth: if tailwater is lower than the conjugate depth, the jump is swept downstream; if higher, it is pushed upstream and may drown the gate.
- Jumps also aerate water and mix chemicals in treatment works.

Exam tips: compute Fr₁ first; use the conjugate depth equation, not energy; quote the energy loss and comment on its practical significance (scour protection, stilling basin design).

Coastal and offshore engineering needs a description of sea waves. Linear (Airy) wave theory, valid for small-amplitude waves, is the starting point.

Describing a regular wave
- Height H (crest to trough), amplitude a = H/2, period T, wavelength L, water depth h.
- Wave number k = 2π/L, angular frequency ω = 2π/T, phase speed (celerity) c = L/T = ω/k.
- Steepness H/L; relative depth h/L.

The dispersion relation
ω² = gk tanh(kh)
Waves of different periods travel at different speeds (they are dispersive), and the wavelength for a given period depends on the depth. The equation must usually be solved by iteration (or with tables or approximations).

Deep and shallow water limits
- Deep water (h > L/2, tanh(kh) ≈ 1): L₀ = gT²/(2π) ≈ 1.56T² (metres, T in seconds); c₀ = gT/(2π) ≈ 1.56T. Example: T = 10 s gives L₀ ≈ 156 m and c₀ ≈ 15.6 m/s.
- Shallow water (h < L/20, tanh(kh) ≈ kh): c = √(gh), independent of period. Example: at h = 5 m, c ≈ 7.0 m/s.
- In between (intermediate depth) use the full relation. For T = 10 s in 10 m of water, L ≈ 92 m (kh ≈ 0.68).

Water particle motion
- Under a wave, water particles move in orbits: circles in deep water, flattening to ellipses in intermediate and shallow water.
- In deep water the orbit radius decays with depth as e^(kz) (z negative downwards from the still water level): at a depth of half a wavelength the motion is only about 4% of its surface value. This is why deep-water waves "do not feel" the bed.
- Surface horizontal velocity amplitude in deep water: u₀ = ωH/2 = πH/T; acceleration amplitude ω²H/2.

Energy and group velocity
- Mean wave energy per unit surface area: E = ρgH²/8. For H = 2 m in sea water, E ≈ 5.0 kJ/m².
- Energy travels at the group velocity c_g = nc, where n = ½ in deep water and n → 1 in shallow water.
- Energy flux (power per metre of crest) P = E c_g, the basis of wave energy resource estimates.

Transformation towards the shore
- Shoaling: as waves enter shallower water, c_g changes and the height changes to keep the energy flux constant (eventually increasing).
- Refraction: crests bend to become more parallel to the depth contours, because the part in shallower water travels more slowly.
- Diffraction: energy spreads into the sheltered zone behind breakwaters.
- Breaking: in deep water waves break when steepness H/L exceeds about 1/7; in shallow water when H exceeds about 0.78h.

Limits of linear theory
It assumes small H/L and H/h. Steep or very shallow-water waves need nonlinear theories (Stokes, cnoidal, solitary). Real seas are irregular and are described statistically by the significant wave height H_s and spectra.

Exam tips: always decide first whether the water is deep, shallow or intermediate (compare h with L); for intermediate depths iterate the dispersion relation; quote units carefully (c in m/s, L in m).

notes.h: Wave loads on offshore structures: the Morison equation
notes.body:
Offshore platforms, wind-turbine monopiles, jetty piles and pipelines must resist wave forces. For members that are slender compared with the wavelength, the standard design tool is the Morison equation (Morison, O'Brien, Johnson and Schaaf, 1950).

When does Morison apply?
- The member must be small compared with the wavelength: D/L less than about 0.2. Then the wave is not significantly altered (diffracted) by the member, and the flow at the member can be taken as the undisturbed wave flow.
- Large structures (gravity-base platforms, big caissons) with D/L above about 0.2 need diffraction theory instead.

The Morison equation (force per unit length of a vertical cylinder)
F = ½ρC_D D|u|u + ρC_M (πD²/4) du/dt
- The first term is drag, proportional to velocity squared (written |u|u so that it changes sign with the flow direction).
- The second term is inertia, proportional to the fluid acceleration. C_M = 1 + C_a: the "1" is the Froude–Krylov force from the pressure gradient that accelerates the water, and C_a (about 1 for a circular cylinder) is the added-mass effect of water accelerated around the body.
- C_D and C_M depend on Reynolds number, the Keulegan–Carpenter number KC = u₀T/D and surface roughness (including marine growth). Typical values used in teaching are C_D ≈ 0.6–1.2 and C_M ≈ 1.5–2.0; design codes give specific values.

Phase between the terms
For a linear wave, u = u₀ cos ωt and du/dt = −u₀ω sin ωt, so drag peaks at the crest and trough, while inertia peaks a quarter of a period earlier or later. The two maxima do not add directly. If the inertia amplitude F_I ≥ 2F_D, the maximum total force is F_I; otherwise it is F_D + F_I²/(4F_D).

Worked example
A 1 m diameter pile stands in deep water (ρ = 1025 kg/m³). Regular waves have H = 4 m and T = 8 s. Use C_D = 1.0 and C_M = 2.0, and find the force per metre at the still water level.
- ω = 2π/8 = 0.785 rad/s; L₀ = 1.56 × 64 ≈ 100 m, so D/L ≈ 0.01: Morison applies.
- u₀ = ωH/2 = 1.57 m/s; acceleration amplitude a₀ = ω²H/2 = 1.23 m/s².
- Drag amplitude F_D = ½ × 1025 × 1.0 × 1 × 1.57² ≈ 1.26 kN/m.
- Inertia amplitude F_I = 1025 × 2.0 × (π/4) × 1.23 ≈ 1.99 kN/m.
- Since F_I < 2F_D, F_max = F_D + F_I²/(4F_D) ≈ 1.26 + 0.78 ≈ 2.04 kN/m.
- KC = u₀T/D ≈ 12.6, a regime where both drag and inertia matter.

Total force and overturning moment
Velocity and acceleration decay with depth (e^(kz) in deep water), so the force per unit length is integrated down the member to get the total base shear and overturning moment. Linear theory only gives values up to the still water level; engineers extend the profile up to the actual crest (for example by "stretching" methods) for design.

Other considerations
Current adds to the wave velocity in the drag term; inclined members use the velocity components normal to their axis; groups of members interact; slamming and vortex-induced vibration need separate checks.

Exam tips: check D/L first; compute u₀ and a₀ from linear theory; remember drag and inertia are 90° out of phase in a linear wave; say clearly which coefficients you have assumed.

cards.b: p = p_atm + ρgh in a liquid of constant density, h the depth below the free surface. From dp/dz = −ρg.
h = p/(ρg): pressure expressed as an equivalent height of the liquid. 50 kPa ≈ 5.10 m of water.
About 1025 kg/m³ (fresh water about 1000 kg/m³).
About 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m²/s (dynamic viscosity about 1.0 × 10⁻³ Pa s).
Gauge pressure is measured relative to atmospheric; absolute = gauge + atmospheric (≈ 101 kPa).

cards.f: Why water is treated as incompressible
cards.b: Its bulk modulus (≈ 2.2 GPa) is so large that density changes are negligible for civil engineering pressures (water hammer is the main exception).
Vapour bubbles form where pressure drops below the vapour pressure and collapse violently, damaging spillways, pumps and turbines.

cards.f: Water thrust on a vertical wall per metre
cards.b: F = ρgh²/2, acting at h/3 above the base (the centroid of the triangular pressure diagram).

cards.f: Force on any submerged plane surface
cards.b: F = ρ g h_c A, where h_c is the depth of the centroid; acts at the centre of pressure, which is below the centroid unless the surface is horizontal.

cards.f: Vertical component on a curved surface
cards.b: Equal to the weight of water (real or imaginary) vertically above the surface up to the free-surface level.

cards.f: Why radial gates are hinged at the centre of curvature
cards.b: Pressure acts normal to the arc, so the resultant passes through the centre; it has no moment about the hinge, making the gate easier to operate.

cards.f: Factor of safety against overturning (gravity dam)
cards.b: Restoring moment of the dam's weight about the toe divided by the overturning moment of water thrust (plus uplift).
If the resultant on the base lies within the middle third (eccentricity ≤ B/6), base pressure is compressive everywhere.
Upward water pressure on the base from seepage; commonly assumed triangular from full head at the heel to tailwater at the toe. Reduces stability.
p/(ρg) + V²/(2g) + z = H, constant along a streamline for steady, inviscid, incompressible flow.

cards.f: Energy equation with losses and machines
cards.b: H₁ + h_pump = H₂ + h_turbine + h_L, all in metres of head.
Q = C_d a √(2gH); C_d ≈ 0.6 for a sharp-edged orifice.
The narrowest section of a jet just downstream of a sharp-edged orifice, where streamlines become parallel; its area is smaller than the orifice.

cards.f: Energy grade line vs hydraulic grade line
cards.b: EGL plots total head H; HGL plots p/(ρg) + z, one velocity head V²/(2g) below the EGL.

cards.f: Time to drain a tank through an orifice
cards.b: t = 2A_t(√H₁ − √H₂)/(C_d a √(2g)), from continuity and Q = C_d a √(2gH).

cards.f: Continuity in an open channel per unit width
cards.b: q = Vy is constant along a channel of constant width (q in m²/s).
ΣF = ρQ(V_out − V_in), applied as a vector to the fluid in a control volume.

cards.f: Hydrostatic force on a channel section per metre width
cards.b: ρgy²/2, valid where streamlines are straight and parallel.

cards.f: Discharge under a sluice gate (no losses)
cards.b: q = y₁y₂√[2g/(y₁ + y₂)], from Bernoulli and continuity between upstream and vena contracta.

cards.f: Force on a sluice gate per metre width
cards.b: F = ½ρg(y₁² − y₂²) − ρq(V₂ − V₁).

cards.f: Why pipe bends need thrust blocks
cards.b: Changing flow direction and the pressure forces at each end produce a resultant force on the bend that the joints alone may not resist.

cards.f: When to use momentum rather than energy
cards.b: When there are unknown internal energy losses (e.g. hydraulic jumps, sudden expansions) or when a force on a structure is needed.
Re = VD/ν: laminar below about 2000, turbulent above about 4000 in pipes. Water mains are nearly always turbulent.
h_f = f(L/D)V²/(2g). For laminar flow f = 64/Re.
1/√f = −2 log₁₀[k_s/(3.7D) + 2.51/(Re√f)]: turbulent friction factor in commercial pipes; basis of the Moody diagram.

cards.f: Effect of halving pipe diameter at fixed Q and f
cards.b: Friction head loss increases 32 times, since h_f ∝ Q²/D⁵.
Same head loss across each branch; total flow is the sum of branch flows.
Where the pump's head–flow curve crosses the system curve (static lift + losses ∝ Q²).
R = A/P: flow area divided by wetted perimeter (free surface not included). Rectangular channel: by/(b + 2y).
V = (1/n)R^(2/3)S^(1/2) in SI units, for uniform (normal) flow.

cards.f: Froude number in a rectangular channel
cards.b: Fr = V/√(gy). Subcritical if Fr < 1, supercritical if Fr > 1, critical if Fr = 1.
E = y + V²/(2g) = y + q²/(2gy²) (rectangular channel), measured above the bed.

cards.f: Critical depth in a rectangular channel
cards.b: y_c = (q²/g)^(1/3); at critical flow E_min = 1.5y_c and V_c = √(gy_c).
The subcritical and supercritical depths that have the same specific energy for a given q.
Q = b√g(2H/3)^(3/2) ≈ 1.705bH^(3/2) in SI units, H the upstream energy head above the crest.

cards.f: Where subcritical and supercritical flows are controlled from
cards.b: Subcritical: from downstream (weirs, reservoirs). Supercritical: from upstream (sluice gates, steep inlets).
An abrupt transition from supercritical to subcritical flow with a rise in depth, intense turbulence and energy loss.
y₂/y₁ = ½[√(1 + 8Fr₁²) − 1], from the momentum equation for a horizontal rectangular channel with bed friction neglected.

cards.f: Energy loss in a hydraulic jump
cards.b: ΔE = (y₂ − y₁)³/(4y₁y₂), for a jump in a horizontal rectangular channel (y₁, y₂ the conjugate depths).

cards.f: Why the momentum equation is used across a jump
cards.b: The jump's turbulent energy loss is unknown, so energy cannot be conserved; momentum is conserved with only hydrostatic end forces.
To force a stable hydraulic jump that dissipates energy below a spillway or gate, protecting the bed downstream from scour.

cards.f: Preferred Froude range for stilling basin jumps
cards.b: About 4.5 to 9 (steady jump); 2.5–4.5 gives oscillating, wave-producing jumps.
ω² = gk tanh(kh), with ω = 2π/T and k = 2π/L.
L₀ = gT²/(2π) ≈ 1.56T² m. T = 10 s gives about 156 m. Deep water when h > L/2.
c = √(gh), independent of period; applies when h < L/20.
E = ρgH²/8 (mean energy per unit surface area, linear theory).
Speed at which wave energy travels: c_g = nc, with n = ½ in deep water and 1 in shallow water.

cards.f: Decay of particle motion with depth (deep water)
cards.b: Orbit size ∝ e^(kz); at z = −L/2 the motion is about 4% of the surface value.
Waves break roughly when H exceeds about 0.78 times the local depth.
Bending of wave crests towards alignment with depth contours, because waves travel slower in shallower water.
Force per unit length F = ½ρC_D D|u|u + ρC_M(πD²/4)du/dt: drag term plus inertia term.
For slender members, D/L less than about 0.2, so the structure does not significantly diffract the waves.
C_M = 1 + C_a: Froude–Krylov (pressure gradient) part plus added-mass coefficient (≈ 1 for a circular cylinder).
KC = u₀T/D. Low KC: inertia dominates; high KC: drag dominates.

cards.f: Phase of drag and inertia forces in a linear wave
cards.b: Drag peaks with velocity (under crest and trough); inertia peaks with acceleration, a quarter-period apart.
F_max = F_D + F_I²/(4F_D); if F_I ≥ 2F_D, F_max = F_I.

cards.f: Deep-water surface particle velocity and acceleration amplitudes
cards.b: u₀ = ωH/2 = πH/T and a₀ = ω²H/2.

questions.q: What is the gauge pressure 30 m below the surface of the sea (ρ = 1025 kg/m³)?
questions.why: p = ρgh = 1025 × 9.81 × 30 ≈ 302 kPa. 294 kPa uses the density of fresh water. 403 kPa adds atmospheric pressure, giving the absolute rather than the gauge pressure. 30.8 kPa leaves out g (1025 × 30 = 30 750 Pa).

questions.q: A water main has a gauge pressure of 50 kPa. What is this as a pressure head of water?
questions.why: h = p/(ρg) = 50 000/(1000 × 9.81) ≈ 5.10 m of water. 0.375 m uses the density of mercury, giving the head of mercury instead of water. 50 m divides by ρ but forgets g. 4.97 m uses the density of sea water (1025 kg/m³), which is wrong for a fresh-water main.

questions.q: Explain why the pressure at the base of a narrow standpipe and at the base of a wide reservoir is the same when both are filled with water to the same depth, and calculate this pressure for a depth of 12 m.
markScheme: Hydrostatic law dp/dz = −ρg depends only on depth and density
Pressure is independent of container shape/volume (hydrostatic paradox)
p = ρgh = 1000 × 9.81 × 12 ≈ 118 kPa gauge
Extra weight in the reservoir is carried by the larger base area / walls, not by higher pressure
questions.modelAnswer: In still water the hydrostatic law dp/dz = −ρg means pressure increases only with depth and density. Neither the shape nor the volume of the container enters, so the pressure at the base is the same in a narrow standpipe and a wide reservoir if the depth is the same. For 12 m of water, p = ρgh = 1000 × 9.81 × 12 ≈ 118 kPa gauge. The much greater weight of water in the reservoir is supported by its much larger base area (and, where the walls slope, by the walls), not by a higher pressure.

questions.q: Water stands 10 m deep against the vertical upstream face of a dam. What is the horizontal water thrust per metre length?
questions.why: F = ρgh²/2 = 1000 × 9.81 × 100/2 = 490.5 kN/m (the area of the triangular pressure diagram). 981 kN/m forgets the ½, treating the pressure as uniform at its base value. 98.1 kN/m is the pressure at the base, ρgh in kPa, which has not been integrated over the depth. 49.05 kN/m is the mean pressure ρgh/2 without multiplying by the 10 m depth.

questions.q: For the same 10 m deep water against a vertical dam face, what is the overturning moment of the water thrust about the toe (base level), per metre length?
questions.why: The thrust of 490.5 kN/m acts at h/3 = 3.33 m above the base, so M = 490.5 × 3.33 ≈ 1635 kN m/m (= ρgh³/6). 2453 kN m/m places the thrust at mid-depth (5 m), the centroid of the wetted area rather than the centre of pressure. 3270 kN m/m uses 2h/3 = 6.67 m above the base, mixing up the depth of the centre of pressure below the surface with its height above the base. 4905 kN m/m uses the full 10 m lever arm.

questions.q: A quarter-circle radial gate of radius 3 m retains water whose surface is level with the top of the gate; the quarter-circle of water lies vertically above the curved surface. Find the horizontal and vertical components of the water force per metre width, the resultant, and its line of action.
markScheme: F_H = force on vertical projection = ρgR²/2 = 44.1 kN/m
F_V = weight of water above the surface = ρg πR²/4 = 69.3 kN/m
Resultant = √(44.1² + 69.3²) ≈ 82.2 kN/m
Inclined at tan⁻¹(69.3/44.1) ≈ 57.5° to the horizontal
Passes through the centre of curvature (all pressure forces are normal to the arc)
questions.modelAnswer: The horizontal component equals the force on the vertical projection of the gate, a 3 m high rectangle with its top at the surface: F_H = ρgR²/2 = 1000 × 9.81 × 9/2 ≈ 44.1 kN/m, acting 2 m below the surface. The vertical component equals the weight of the quarter-circle of water above the gate: F_V = ρg πR²/4 = 1000 × 9.81 × π × 9/4 ≈ 69.3 kN/m. The resultant is √(44.1² + 69.3²) ≈ 82.2 kN/m, inclined at tan⁻¹(69.3/44.1) ≈ 57.5° to the horizontal. Because every elemental pressure force is normal to the circular surface, the resultant passes through the centre of curvature, which is why such gates are hinged there.

questions.q: A sharp-edged orifice of diameter 50 mm (C_d = 0.62) discharges from a tank under a constant head of 2 m. What is the flow rate?
questions.why: Q = C_d a √(2gH) = 0.62 × 1.963 × 10⁻³ × 6.26 ≈ 0.0076 m³/s = 7.6 L/s. 12.3 L/s is the ideal flow, leaving out C_d. 30.5 L/s uses the diameter as the radius when calculating the area (πd² instead of πd²/4). 5.4 L/s leaves out the 2 in √(2gH).

questions.q: Along a horizontal pipe of constant diameter with friction, how do the energy grade line (EGL) and hydraulic grade line (HGL) behave?
options: Both fall at the same rate and stay a constant velocity head apart
The EGL falls but the HGL stays horizontal
Both stay horizontal because the velocity is constant
The HGL falls and the EGL rises to keep the total constant
questions.why: Friction removes energy, so total head falls steadily; with constant diameter the velocity head V²/2g is constant, so the HGL falls parallel to the EGL. 'EGL falls, HGL horizontal' would need the velocity head to shrink along the pipe, which constant diameter rules out. 'Both horizontal' applies Bernoulli without losses and ignores friction. 'EGL rises' would need energy to be added, as by a pump; total head cannot rise on its own.

questions.q: A tank of plan area 2 m² drains through a 50 mm sharp-edged orifice (C_d = 0.62) in its base. Derive an expression for the time taken for the water level to fall from H₁ to H₂, and calculate the time to fall from 2.0 m to 0.5 m.
markScheme: Continuity: −A_t dH/dt = C_d a √(2gH)
Separate variables: dt = −A_t dH/(C_d a √(2g) √H)
Integrate: t = 2A_t(√H₁ − √H₂)/(C_d a √(2g))
questions.modelAnswer: At any instant the outflow Q = C_d a √(2gH) equals the rate at which the stored volume falls: −A_t dH/dt = C_d a √(2gH). Separating variables, dt = −A_t H^(−1/2) dH/(C_d a √(2g)), and integrating from H₁ to H₂ gives t = 2A_t(√H₁ − √H₂)/(C_d a √(2g)). Here a = π × 0.05²/4 = 1.963 × 10⁻³ m², so C_d a √(2g) = 0.62 × 1.963 × 10⁻³ × 4.429 ≈ 5.39 × 10⁻³ m^2.5/s. Then t = 2 × 2 × (√2 − √0.5)/5.39 × 10⁻³ = 4 × 0.707/5.39 × 10⁻³ ≈ 525 s, about 8.7 minutes. Note this is half the time to empty completely from 2 m, because the flow slows as the head drops.

questions.q: Water flows under a sluice gate from an upstream depth of 2.0 m to a downstream depth of 0.4 m, with q = 2.29 m²/s. What is the horizontal force on the gate per metre width?
questions.why: F = ½ρg(y₁² − y₂²) − ρq(V₂ − V₁) = 18.8 − 1000 × 2.29 × (5.72 − 1.14)/1000 ≈ 18.8 − 10.5 = 8.4 kN/m. 18.8 kN/m is just the difference in hydrostatic forces, ignoring the momentum change. 19.6 kN/m is the hydrostatic thrust of still water 2 m deep (½ρgy₁²), as if no water flowed. 29.3 kN/m adds the momentum term instead of subtracting it, a sign error in the momentum equation.

questions.q: For the same sluice gate (upstream depth 2.0 m, downstream depth 0.4 m), assuming no energy loss, what is the discharge per metre width?
questions.why: Combining Bernoulli and continuity gives q = y₁y₂√[2g/(y₁ + y₂)] = 0.8 × √(19.62/2.4) ≈ 2.29 m²/s. 2.24 m²/s uses y₂√[2g(y₁ − y₂)], which ignores the upstream velocity head. 2.51 m²/s uses y₂√(2gy₁), which ignores both the upstream velocity and the depth (pressure head) downstream. 11.4 m²/s multiplies the downstream velocity by the upstream depth, applying continuity with the wrong depth.

questions.q: Explain, with a control-volume sketch described in words, why the force on a sluice gate is smaller than the hydrostatic force that would act on it if the gate were fully closed with the same upstream depth.
markScheme: Control volume from upstream section (y₁) to vena contracta (y₂)
Forces: ½ρgy₁² downstream, ½ρgy₂² upstream, gate force F_g upstream
Momentum: net force = ρq(V₂ − V₁) > 0 because flow accelerates
So F_g = ½ρg(y₁² − y₂²) − ρq(V₂ − V₁), less than ½ρgy₁²
Physically: pressure on the lower part of the gate drops as water accelerates beneath it (Bernoulli)
questions.modelAnswer: Take a control volume containing the water between an upstream section of depth y₁, where the pressure is hydrostatic, and the vena contracta of depth y₂ just downstream of the gate. The forces on this water in the flow direction are the upstream hydrostatic force ½ρgy₁² (downstream), the downstream hydrostatic force ½ρgy₂² (upstream) and the gate's force F_g (upstream); bed friction is neglected. The water accelerates from V₁ to V₂, so the net force must equal ρq(V₂ − V₁), which is positive. Hence F_g = ½ρg(y₁² − y₂²) − ρq(V₂ − V₁), which is smaller than the closed-gate value ½ρgy₁². Physically, near the gate lip the water speeds up, so by Bernoulli the pressure on the lower part of the gate falls below hydrostatic.

questions.q: A 300 mm main, 1000 m long, carries 0.1 m³/s of water with Darcy friction factor 0.018. What is the friction head loss?
questions.why: V = 0.1/0.0707 = 1.41 m/s and h_f = 0.018 × (1000/0.3) × 1.41²/19.62 ≈ 6.1 m. 4.3 m uses V instead of V². 1.8 m uses L instead of L/D (forgets to divide by the 0.3 m diameter). 60 m confuses the pressure drop of about 60 kPa with a head in metres.

questions.q: At a fixed flow rate and friction factor, the diameter of a pipeline is halved. By what factor does the friction head loss change?
questions.why: h_f = f(L/D)V²/(2g) with V ∝ 1/D², so h_f ∝ 1/D⁵ and halving D gives 2⁵ = 32. 4 times tracks only the fourfold rise in velocity, as if the loss were proportional to V rather than V² and the L/D term were ignored. 16 times includes the V² ∝ 1/D⁴ effect but forgets the extra 1/D in L/D. 2 times includes only the L/D term and forgets that the velocity rises.

questions.q: Explain why the friction factor in turbulent pipe flow depends on both Reynolds number and pipe roughness, and why at very high Reynolds numbers it depends only on roughness.
markScheme: Turbulent flow has a thin viscous sublayer at the wall
At lower Re (smooth turbulent) roughness lies within sublayer: f depends on Re
As Re increases sublayer thins; roughness protrudes, adding form drag: f depends on Re and k_s/D (transitional)
At very high Re roughness dominates; viscous effects negligible: f depends on k_s/D only (rough turbulent)
questions.modelAnswer: In turbulent pipe flow a thin viscous sublayer remains next to the wall. If the roughness elements lie inside this sublayer, the wall behaves as hydraulically smooth and f depends only on Reynolds number. As Re rises the sublayer gets thinner and the roughness starts to poke through it, adding form drag on the roughness elements, so f depends on both Re and k_s/D: this is the transitional zone that the Colebrook–White equation describes. At very high Re the sublayer is much thinner than the roughness, the resistance is dominated by form drag on the roughness and viscosity no longer matters, so f depends only on k_s/D and the Moody curves become horizontal.

questions.q: A wide rectangular channel carries q = 2 m²/s per metre width. What is the critical depth?
questions.why: y_c = (q²/g)^(1/3) = (4/9.81)^(1/3) ≈ 0.742 m. 0.408 m is q²/g without the cube root. 0.639 m takes the square root instead of the cube root. 1.11 m is the minimum specific energy, 1.5y_c, not the critical depth.

questions.q: A rectangular concrete channel 4 m wide has a normal depth of 1.5 m, Manning's n = 0.015 and bed slope 0.001. What is the discharge?
questions.why: A = 6 m², P = 4 + 2 × 1.5 = 7 m, R = 0.857 m, V = (1/0.015) × 0.857^(2/3) × 0.001^(1/2) ≈ 1.90 m/s, Q ≈ 11.4 m³/s. 16.6 m³/s uses the depth (1.5 m) as the hydraulic radius, which is only a fair approximation for very wide channels. 13.4 m³/s counts only one side wall in the wetted perimeter (P = 5.5 m). 0.36 m³/s uses S instead of S^(1/2).

questions.q: Sketch and explain the specific energy curve for a rectangular channel at a fixed discharge per unit width, and use it to explain what happens to the water surface when subcritical flow passes over a small, smooth hump in the bed.
markScheme: E = y + q²/(2gy²); curve with minimum at critical depth; asymptotes E = y and y → 0
Two alternate depths for each E > E_min: upper limb subcritical, lower limb supercritical
Over a hump of height Δz (no losses) E falls by Δz
Subcritical flow moves down the upper limb towards critical: depth decreases and the water surface dips over the hump
If Δz exceeds E₁ − E_min, the flow chokes: critical depth on the hump and the upstream level rises
questions.modelAnswer: For fixed q, E = y + q²/(2gy²). At large depth E approaches y (the velocity head is small); as y tends to zero the velocity head grows without limit. Between these the curve has a minimum E_min = 1.5y_c at the critical depth y_c = (q²/g)^(1/3). Each E above the minimum corresponds to two alternate depths: the upper limb is subcritical flow and the lower limb supercritical. When flow passes over a smooth hump of height Δz with negligible losses, the total head is unchanged, so the specific energy measured from the raised bed falls by Δz. For subcritical flow this moves the point down the upper limb towards the minimum: the depth decreases and the water surface dips over the hump. If Δz is larger than E₁ − E_min the flow cannot pass with the original upstream energy; the flow becomes critical on the hump (choked) and the water upstream backs up until there is enough energy to pass the discharge.

questions.q: Supercritical flow at depth 0.4 m and velocity 5.72 m/s enters a hydraulic jump in a rectangular channel. What is the depth after the jump?
questions.why: Fr₁ = 5.72/√(9.81 × 0.4) = 2.89 and y₂ = (0.4/2)[√(1 + 8 × 2.89²) − 1] ≈ 1.45 m. 0.78 m uses Fr₁ instead of Fr₁² inside the square root. 2.89 m leaves out the factor ½. 2.0 m is the alternate depth with the same specific energy, which assumes energy is conserved across the jump; in reality a jump loses energy, so momentum must be used.

questions.q: For the jump from 0.4 m to 1.45 m depth, what is the head loss in the jump?
questions.why: ΔE = (y₂ − y₁)³/(4y₁y₂) = 1.05³/(4 × 0.4 × 1.45) ≈ 0.49 m. 1.05 m is just the rise in depth, not an energy loss. 1.97 m leaves out the 4 in the denominator. 0 m assumes energy is conserved, which is not true for a jump.

questions.q: Starting from the momentum equation, derive the conjugate depth relation y₂/y₁ = ½[√(1 + 8Fr₁²) − 1] for a hydraulic jump in a horizontal rectangular channel.
markScheme: CV around the jump; neglect bed friction; forces ½ρgy₁² and ½ρgy₂² per unit width
½ρg(y₁² − y₂²) = ρq(V₂ − V₁) with V = q/y
Simplify: ½g(y₁ + y₂)(y₁ − y₂) = q²(y₁ − y₂)/(y₁y₂) → q²/g = y₁y₂(y₁ + y₂)/2
Divide by y₁³ with Fr₁² = q²/(gy₁³): (y₂/y₁)² + (y₂/y₁) − 2Fr₁² = 0
Positive root: y₂/y₁ = ½[√(1 + 8Fr₁²) − 1]
questions.modelAnswer: Take a control volume around the jump on a horizontal bed and neglect bed friction over its short length. Per metre width the only horizontal forces are the hydrostatic forces ½ρgy₁² (downstream) and ½ρgy₂² (upstream). Momentum: ½ρg(y₁² − y₂²) = ρq(V₂ − V₁), with V₁ = q/y₁ and V₂ = q/y₂. The right side is ρq²(1/y₂ − 1/y₁) = ρq²(y₁ − y₂)/(y₁y₂). Dividing both sides by ρ(y₁ − y₂): ½g(y₁ + y₂) = q²/(y₁y₂), so q²/g = y₁y₂(y₁ + y₂)/2. With Fr₁² = q²/(gy₁³) and r = y₂/y₁, dividing by y₁³ gives Fr₁² = r(1 + r)/2, i.e. r² + r − 2Fr₁² = 0. The positive root is r = ½[√(1 + 8Fr₁²) − 1].

questions.q: What is the deep-water wavelength of a regular wave of period 10 s?
questions.why: L₀ = gT²/(2π) = 9.81 × 100/6.283 ≈ 156 m. 15.6 m is gT/(2π), which is the deep-water wave speed in m/s, not the wavelength. 981 m is gT², forgetting to divide by 2π. 24.8 m divides by 4π² instead of 2π.

questions.q: What is the speed of a shallow-water wave in water 5 m deep?
questions.why: c = √(gh) = √(9.81 × 5) ≈ 7.0 m/s. 49.1 m/s is gh without the square root. 9.9 m/s is √(2gh), the Torricelli jet speed, which is a different physical result. 2.2 m/s is √h, forgetting g.

questions.q: Using the dispersion relation, show that wave speed is independent of period in shallow water and depends on period in deep water. State the depth criteria used for each limit.
markScheme: c = ω/k; dispersion ω² = gk tanh(kh) gives c² = (g/k) tanh(kh)
Deep water (kh large, h > L/2): tanh(kh) ≈ 1 so c² = g/k = gL/(2π)
With L = cT this gives c = gT/(2π): depends on period
Shallow water (kh small, h < L/20): tanh(kh) ≈ kh so c² = gh
c = √(gh): depends only on depth, not period (non-dispersive)
questions.modelAnswer: The phase speed is c = ω/k, and the dispersion relation ω² = gk tanh(kh) gives c² = (g/k) tanh(kh). In deep water, where h is greater than about half a wavelength, kh is large and tanh(kh) ≈ 1, so c² = g/k = gL/(2π). Since L = cT, this becomes c = gT/(2π): longer-period waves travel faster, so deep-water waves are dispersive (which is why long swell arrives ahead of shorter waves from a distant storm). In shallow water, where h is less than about a twentieth of a wavelength, kh is small and tanh(kh) ≈ kh, so c² = gh and c = √(gh), which depends only on the depth and not on the period: shallow-water waves are non-dispersive.

questions.q: A 1 m diameter pile in deep sea water (ρ = 1025 kg/m³) is struck by regular waves of height 4 m and period 8 s. With C_M = 2.0, what is the amplitude of the inertia force per metre at the still water level?
questions.why: a₀ = ω²H/2 = 0.785² × 2 = 1.23 m/s², so F_I = ρC_M(πD²/4)a₀ = 1025 × 2.0 × 0.785 × 1.23 ≈ 1.99 kN/m. 0.99 kN/m uses C_M = 1, keeping only the Froude–Krylov part and leaving out added mass. 1.26 kN/m is the drag force amplitude with C_D = 1, not the inertia force. 2.53 kN/m uses D² instead of πD²/4 for the cross-sectional area.

questions.q: Under which condition is the Morison equation an appropriate way to estimate wave forces on a member?
options: The member diameter is small compared with the wavelength (D/L below about 0.2)
The wave height is small compared with the water depth
The water is deep (h greater than L/2)
questions.why: Morison assumes the member does not disturb the incident wave field, which holds for slender members with D/L below about 0.2. 'Wave height small compared with depth' is a condition for linear wave theory, not for using Morison. A KC below 1 just means inertia dominates; Morison still applies (with the drag term small), so it is not the criterion. Deep water is not required: Morison is used in any depth, with velocities from a suitable wave theory.

questions.q: For the pile in the worked example (D = 1 m, H = 4 m, T = 8 s, deep water, C_D = 1.0, C_M = 2.0, ρ = 1025 kg/m³), the drag and inertia amplitudes at the still water level are 1.26 kN/m and 1.99 kN/m. Explain why the maximum force is not their sum and calculate it.
markScheme: u = u₀ cos ωt, du/dt = −u₀ω sin ωt: velocity and acceleration 90° out of phase
F(θ) = F_D cos θ|cos θ| + F_I sin θ (with suitable phase reference)
Maximise: since F_I < 2F_D, max where sin θ = F_I/(2F_D)
Comparison: less than F_D + F_I = 3.25 kN/m
questions.modelAnswer: In a linear wave the horizontal velocity and acceleration are a quarter-period out of phase: when the velocity (and drag) is greatest under the crest, the acceleration (and inertia force) is zero, and vice versa. So the two amplitudes never occur together and cannot simply be added. Writing the force as F(θ) = F_D cos θ|cos θ| + F_I sin θ and maximising over the half-cycle where cos θ > 0 gives sin θ = F_I/(2F_D) when F_I < 2F_D, and then F_max = F_D + F_I²/(4F_D). Here F_I/(2F_D) = 0.79 < 1, so F_max = 1.26 + 1.99²/(4 × 1.26) ≈ 1.26 + 0.78 ≈ 2.04 kN/m, well below the 3.25 kN/m given by adding the amplitudes.

questions.q:
A concrete gravity dam (density 2400 kg/m³) has a rectangular cross-section 10 m high and 7 m wide at the base. The reservoir behind it is level with the crest (10 m deep) and there is no water downstream. Work per metre length of dam, take g = 9.81 m/s².
(a) Calculate the horizontal water thrust and its line of action. [3]
(b) Calculate the factor of safety against overturning about the toe, ignoring uplift. [4]
(c) Calculate the factor of safety against sliding if the coefficient of friction on the base is 0.6, ignoring uplift. [2]
(d) Repeat (b) and (c) allowing for uplift that varies linearly from full reservoir head at the heel to zero at the toe. [6]
(e) Check whether the resultant lies within the middle third of the base, with and without uplift, and comment on the base pressures. [5]
markScheme: (a) F = ρgh²/2 = 490.5 kN/m, acting 3.33 m above the base
(b) W = 2400 × 9.81 × 70 = 1648 kN/m at 3.5 m from toe; M_R = 5768 kN m/m; M_O = 1635 kN m/m; FoS ≈ 3.5
(d) Uplift U = ½ × 9.81 × 10 × 7 ≈ 343 kN/m acting B/3 from heel (4.67 m from toe)
(e) No uplift: x = (5768 − 1635)/1648 ≈ 2.51 m from toe, e ≈ 0.99 m < B/6 = 1.17 m: inside middle third
(e) σ = (V/B)(1 ± 6e/B): toe ≈ 436 kPa, heel ≈ 35 kPa (all compression)
(e) With uplift: x ≈ 1.94 m, e ≈ 1.56 m > B/6: outside middle third, tension predicted at heel (≈ −63 kPa); a crack could open and increase uplift, so drains or a wider base are needed
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Per metre length, F = ρgh²/2 = 1000 × 9.81 × 10²/2 = 490.5 kN/m, acting at the centroid of the triangular pressure diagram, h/3 = 3.33 m above the base.

(b) The dam's weight W = 2400 × 9.81 × (10 × 7) = 1648 kN/m, acting through the centre of the base, 3.5 m from the toe. Restoring moment about the toe M_R = 1648 × 3.5 = 5768 kN m/m. Overturning moment M_O = 490.5 × 3.33 = 1635 kN m/m. Factor of safety against overturning = 5768/1635 ≈ 3.5.

(c) Sliding factor of safety = μW/F = 0.6 × 1648/490.5 ≈ 2.0.

(d) Uplift varies from ρgh = 98.1 kPa at the heel to zero at the toe, so U = ½ × 98.1 × 7 ≈ 343 kN/m, acting at the centroid of the triangle, B/3 = 2.33 m from the heel, i.e. 4.67 m from the toe. Its moment about the toe is 343 × 4.67 ≈ 1602 kN m/m, which adds to overturning: M_O = 1635 + 1602 = 3237 kN m/m. Factor of safety against overturning = 5768/3237 ≈ 1.78. Sliding: 0.6 × (1648 − 343)/490.5 ≈ 1.60. Uplift roughly halves the overturning margin.

(e) Without uplift, the net vertical force is V = 1648 kN/m and its distance from the toe is x = (M_R − M_O)/V = (5768 − 1635)/1648 ≈ 2.51 m. The eccentricity from the base centre is e = 3.5 − 2.51 = 0.99 m, which is less than B/6 = 1.17 m, so the resultant is inside the middle third. Base pressures σ = (V/B)(1 ± 6e/B) = 235.4 × (1 ± 0.85) give about 436 kPa at the toe and 35 kPa at the heel: compression everywhere.
With uplift, V = 1648 − 343 = 1305 kN/m and x = (5768 − 3237)/1305 ≈ 1.94 m, so e ≈ 1.56 m, outside the middle third. The linear distribution then predicts about 436 kPa at the toe and tension of about 63 kPa at the heel. Concrete–rock joints carry little tension, so a crack could open at the heel, letting full reservoir pressure in and increasing uplift further. The design should be improved, for example with drainage galleries to cut uplift, a wider base or a sloping upstream face whose water load adds vertical weight.

questions.q:
A vertical sluice gate controls flow in a horizontal rectangular channel. Upstream of the gate the depth is 2.0 m; at the vena contracta just downstream the depth is 0.4 m. Assume no energy loss between these two sections and take g = 9.81 m/s².
(a) Find the discharge per metre width and the velocities upstream and at the vena contracta. [5]
(b) Find the horizontal force on the gate per metre width. [5]
(c) Show that the flow at the vena contracta is supercritical. [2]
(d) A hydraulic jump forms downstream. Find the depth after the jump and the head lost in it. [6]
(e) Explain why the tailwater depth matters for where the jump forms. [2]
markScheme: (a) Energy y₁ + V₁²/2g = y₂ + V₂²/2g with continuity → q = y₁y₂√[2g/(y₁ + y₂)] ≈ 2.29 m²/s
(b) Momentum: F = ½ρg(y₁² − y₂²) − ρq(V₂ − V₁) ≈ 18.8 − 10.5 ≈ 8.4 kN/m (downstream on the gate)
(d) ΔE = (y₃ − y₂)³/(4y₂y₃) ≈ 0.49 m (check: E₂ − E₃ = 2.07 − 1.57)
(e) If tailwater < conjugate depth jump moves downstream (scour risk); if greater, jump is pushed upstream and may drown the gate
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) With no losses, y₁ + V₁²/(2g) = y₂ + V₂²/(2g), and continuity gives V₁ = q/y₁, V₂ = q/y₂. Substituting, y₁ − y₂ = (q²/2g)(1/y₂² − 1/y₁²), which rearranges to q = y₁y₂√[2g/(y₁ + y₂)] = 2.0 × 0.4 × √(19.62/2.4) ≈ 2.29 m²/s. Then V₁ = 2.29/2.0 ≈ 1.14 m/s and V₂ = 2.29/0.4 ≈ 5.72 m/s. Check: E₁ = 2.0 + 1.14²/19.62 ≈ 2.07 m and E₂ = 0.4 + 5.72²/19.62 ≈ 2.07 m.

(b) Take a control volume from the upstream section to the vena contracta, with F_g the force of the gate on the water acting upstream. Momentum per metre width: ½ρgy₁² − ½ρgy₂² − F_g = ρq(V₂ − V₁). The hydrostatic terms give ½ × 9810 × (4.0 − 0.16) ≈ 18 835 N/m; the momentum change is 1000 × 2.29 × (5.72 − 1.14) ≈ 10 464 N/m. So F_g ≈ 8370 N/m: the water pushes the gate downstream with about 8.4 kN per metre width.

(c) Fr₂ = V₂/√(gy₂) = 5.72/√(9.81 × 0.4) = 5.72/1.98 ≈ 2.89 > 1, so the flow is supercritical. (Upstream, Fr₁ = 1.14/√(9.81 × 2) ≈ 0.26, subcritical.)

(d) Conjugate depth: y₃ = (0.4/2)[√(1 + 8 × 2.89²) − 1] = 0.2 × (√67.7 − 1) ≈ 0.2 × 7.23 ≈ 1.45 m. Head loss ΔE = (1.45 − 0.4)³/(4 × 0.4 × 1.45) ≈ 1.141/2.31 ≈ 0.49 m. Check: V₃ = 2.29/1.45 ≈ 1.58 m/s, E₃ = 1.45 + 1.58²/19.62 ≈ 1.57 m, and 2.07 − 1.57 = 0.49 m. About a quarter of the energy is dissipated.

(e) The jump forms where the supercritical depth's conjugate matches the actual tailwater depth set by downstream controls. If the tailwater is lower than 1.45 m, the jump is swept downstream, possibly beyond the protected apron, causing scour. If it is higher, the jump is pushed upstream against the gate and becomes a drowned (submerged) jump, which changes the gate's discharge. Stilling basins are designed so the tailwater holds the jump in place.
